newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end higher, weak claims aids rally.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end higher, weak claims aids rally.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended an excruciatingly dull session moderately higher on Thursday, helped out by weak economic data and tame comments from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, players said.

Treasuries spent most of the session meandering in narrow ranges amid low liquidity and as most investors wished to wait for Friday's release of fourth-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) figures before taking on any new positions.
In late trading, the 30-year bond was at 95-10/32, up 15/32 -- its session high. Its yield fell to 6.87 percent from 6.91 percent.

"The market has a good tone. All it needs is buyers, which have been absent for the last couple weeks," said Neil DeSarno, head trader at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp. "If upcoming data show the economy growing but not overheating, maybe after tomorrow, we can break out more on the upside."

Traders said the recent string of weak economic data should have pushed Treasury prices higher. But with the market anticipating strong data in the near-term and more supply on the horizon, players said the bears outnumber the bulls.
Still, Treasury prices rose for third straight day on Thursday.

Treasuries began the day already higher on buying during the Tokyo and London sessions and moved as much a half-point higher after the Labor Department reported a rise in initial jobless claims in the week ended January 25 to 351,000 from a revised 341,000 in the prior week.
The market was further boosted by talk of European central bank buying.

But lack of follow-through buying erased much of the gains. Traders said much of the session's activity was dominated by so-called day traders, who were looking for an excuse to drive up prices and then take profits.
"The market was real choppy and directionless at this point," said one senior trader at a primary dealership. "No one is trading with any conviction or confidence."

Treasuries were once again helped by a fall in the American Production and Inventory Control Society (APICS) manufacturing index to 45.9 in January from 51.8 in December. And, Greenspan's speech to the Senate Finance Committee was deemed bond-friendly, since he didn't talk about overall economic activity.
"Greenspan's testimony was more of the same," said CIBC's DeSarno.

Greenspan told the Senate Finance Committee that the consumer price index is overstated by 0.5 to 1.5 points a year, but the Fed takes that into account in policy debates. He also said policymakers consider exchange rates when deciding monetary policy and noted a stronger dollar tends to keep import prices lower.

Just about the only action was seen in the 10-year inflation-protected note, auctioned Wednesday. The note ended at 100-4/32 to yield 3.36 percent, but not before swinging as low as 100 and as high as 100-17/32.

Meanwhile, the Treasury's $19.25 billion 52-week bill sale didn't go over that well, traders said. The issue was sold at an average discount rate of 5.34 percent and a stop-out rate of 5.35 percent, a one-basis point tail.
The when-issued year-bill was at 5.325 percent late Thursday. Overall, bill rates were one basis point lower to one basis point higher.
Two-year notes rose 1/32 to 99-24/32, yielding 6.01 percent. Five-year notes climbed 5/32 to 99-20/32, yielding 6.34 percent. Ten-year notes rose 8/32 to 99-12/32, yielding 6.59 percent.

Even after trading up the past few sessions, traders said the market remains range-bound. Some noted that the March bond contract is trading in the middle of its recently-established range of 109-26/32 to 111-4/32, ending the day at 110-21/32.
Given the higher liquidity in the futures market, traders said the cash market is taking cues from futures.
Players said it will take a GDP number far from expectations for bonds to break out of the range.
GDP is expected to have risen at a 3.9 percent growth rate in the fourth quarter, according to a Reuters poll. The price deflator is seen up 2.2 percent.
